title: A second inhibitory input reduced model residual by at least 0.05 in one of 11 selected Allen slice panels
abstract: We tested ideal linear cancellation at targets with one excitatory and two inhibitory inputs in Allen Synaptic Physiology r2.1 slice data. Eleven target-and-voltage panels used 33 passed current-clamp fits from 10 targets and nine inferred donors. With finite rise and measured onsets, separate nonnegative inhibitory gains reduced mean residual energy from 0.20520 to 0.19790 of excitatory-input energy. Only one panel had a reduction of at least 0.05. Seven panels used only one input at the optimum. A common gain that kept the measured inhibitory amplitude ratio gave mean residual 0.36315 and was worse than the best single input in nine panels. An overlap criterion explains when a second input helps. Independent sampled-kernel least squares agreed within 8.12e-09. These are conditional model calculations, not measured cancellation. Sparse selected slice circuits, fit error, separate stimulation, and linear voltage addition prevent population or intact-brain claims. The two human panels share one target and donor. Code, extracted records, hashes, source links, checks, and a figure support reproduction.

display.caption: All 11 selected target-and-voltage panels. Separate nonnegative gains improve over the best single input in four panels. A common gain keeps the measured inhibitory amplitude ratio. Blue is mouse VisP and brown is human TCx. Values are model residual energy divided by excitatory energy.

citations.reason: Single-inhibitory-input cancellation model motivated the new two-input gain test. No evidence or code reused.
Finite-rise common-holding component-fit analysis supplied a design precedent. We test two inhibitory gains with new code and extraction.
Prior strength-delay analysis screened during question selection.
